texte.1a082dfb9b93: The bishop on d3 is aiming at h7, and the knight on f3 can go to g5. Check the three conditions for a king attack with same-side castling. What happens after {z1}? What would White have to achieve first?
texte.1775b9dd2d71: Condition 1, the center: not met. There is tension between d4 and c5, nothing is locked, and Black has the counterstrike {z1} ready. The knight on c6 and the queen on d6 support it; the pawn on d4 and the knight on f3 hold it back. Condition 2, superior force: not met. The bishop on d3 does aim at h7, and no black bishop guards the square g5 anymore, but the knight on f6 defends h7 and h5. So {z2} is simply met by {z3}, and White has given a bishop for a pawn. Condition 3, the target: not met. The square h7, at which the bishop aims, is defended by the king and the knight; the square g7 is defended only by the king, but no white piece can reach it. There is no hook either. What is missing: the knight on f6 would have to be driven away or traded, and the center would have to be fixed, as in {v1}. White can achieve both only through the center, with the lever {z4} or with a knight on e5. Remember: a bishop aimed at h7 is not yet an attack. As long as the knight on f6 stays, you work in the center first.
texte.af539fb0c89a: None of the three conditions is met: the center is open, and the knight on f6 defends h7 and h5. After 10. Bxh7+? Nxh7, White is simply a piece down; first White has to drive away the knight on f6 through the center (e3-e4 or Ne5).
texte.1083d6955455: White played {z1} before developing the bishop to e3. Which black move did White prevent in advance? Name the move and its goal. Why is {z2} nevertheless not a mere precautionary move?
texte.6f5350358b47: Without {z1}, Black could attack the bishop on e3 with {z2}. White would have to move the bishop away or allow the trade {z3}. After {z4}, White would have gotten doubled pawns on the e-file (Chapter 5) and lost the bishop pair. The pawn on f3 takes the square g4 away from the knight: if it goes there anyway, {z5} captures it. {z6} is not a mere precautionary move, because it also defends the pawn on e4 and prepares White's plan: {z7}, queenside castling, and a pawn storm on the kingside. {z8} had the same purpose in the Yugoslav Attack of the Dragon Variation ({v1}). Remember: the best prophylaxis prevents a concrete move by your opponent and at the same time furthers your own plan.
texte.8f8b60b778ff: 5. f3 prevents ...Ng4, which would attack the bishop on e3 and cost the bishop pair. At the same time f3 defends the pawn on e4 and prepares Qd2, queenside castling, and the pawn storm: good prophylaxis also furthers your own plan.
texte.ab4229e1ac6f: Apply the third plan question for both sides: which white piece and which black piece has the fewest tasks? Where does it belong, and by which route does it get there?
texte.cf3f61be4193: White: the knight on d2. Of its six squares, e4 and f3 are occupied by White's own pieces, and b3 and c4 are guarded by the black pawns on a4 and b5. Only b1 and f1 remain. Its route leads via f1 to g3 (e3 is occupied by White's own bishop), from where it supports the kingside and defends e4. Unlike in the Italian Game ({v1}), f1 is already free here, since the rook already stands on e1. The rook on a1 has no task yet either, but it can only join in once a file opens. The knight, by contrast, already has a route today. Black: the rook on a8. The pawn on b5 already defends the pawn on a4, so the rook has nothing to do. There is no pawn left on the c-file, so it is open, and the queen on c7 already stands there. With {z1}, the rook therefore gets behind the queen in a single move. A second candidate is the bishop on e7: the pawns on d6 and e5 stand on its color, so it is the bad bishop from Chapter 5. Regrouping it, however, takes several moves. Remember: the knight route d2–f1–g3 is a standard maneuver in the quiet e4 openings, and a rook without a file is almost always the first candidate for the LAP principle.
texte.24ba8a1cf1e1: For White, the knight on d2 has the fewest tasks; it goes via f1 to g3 and supports the kingside. For Black, it is the rook on a8, which reaches the open c-file in one move with ...Rac8.
texte.5cdd10a890d9: First carry out the skeleton X-ray: what has {z1} changed in the skeleton? Then draw up the plan balance for both sides.
texte.cf90fbbddd46: Skeleton X-ray: White no longer has a d-pawn, so the d-file is half-open for White, and the pawn on d6 stands on it. It fails the protection test: the c-pawn is already on c6 and the e-pawn on e5, so neither can ever defend d6. Nor can d6 advance, because the pawns on c4 and e4 guard d5. So d6 is a backward pawn on a half-open file (Chapter 5). White's pawn on e6 is just as weak, because no white pawn can defend it as long as Black's pawn on f5 holds up the f-pawn. In return, though, it cramps Black's pieces. Plan balance: Where? White plays against d6 and on the queenside with {z1}, Black on the kingside and against e6. What does the opponent want? White has to reckon with {z2}, after which the f-file is half-open for the rook on f8, and Black has to keep an eye on the pressure against d6. Which piece? After a queen move, White brings the rooks to the d-file, and Black attacks e6 with the queen from c8 and uses the rook on f8. The plan in one sentence, White: “I use the wedge on e6, attack d6, and secure e4.” Black: “I use the f-file, attack e6, and secure d6.” Remember: after every pawn trade the skeleton X-ray starts over, since a new skeleton brings new plans.
texte.0868d199ab16: Plan balance after the pawn trade
texte.f846e7d39ee7: After 15. dxe6, d6 is a backward pawn on a half-open file; the wedge on e6 is weak but cramps Black. White plays against d6 and on the queenside, Black via the f-file and against e6.
texte.44dc75d67bc9: White is a knight up. With which move does Black save the draw, and which rule from this chapter leads you to it? What would White have played if it had been White's move?
texte.0f2c171c06fc: {z1} Black trades off White's last pawn. After {z2} or {z3}, rook and knight against rook remain. With accurate defense that is a draw, because without pawns White can no longer get a queen. Every other move loses, including {z4}, because White then keeps the h-pawn. The rule behind it: whoever has less material trades pawns. If it were White's move, White would capture on g5 itself, with the pawn or with the knight: both moves keep a pawn, and only they win. Remember: the defender does not count the pieces but the opponent's pawns, since an extra piece without pawns is often worth nothing.
texte.0a08da8c44a1: Whoever has less material trades pawns
texte.8ce1e1879d75: 1... gxh4+! trades off White's last pawn; rook and knight against rook is a draw without pawns. If it were White's move, White would capture on g5 itself and keep a pawn.
